content.title: Rory McIlroy wins second straight Masters, sixth major championship
content.text: Updated April 12, 2026, 10:59 p.m. ETAUGUSTA, Ga. – In the warm, fading light at Augusta National Golf Club, Rory McIlroy slipped into the Green Jacket again at the award ceremony at the 90th Masters.Club Chairman Fred Ridley smiled and said, “Rory, you continue to wear the jacket really well.”“It still fits, which is nice,” McIlroy said.A year ago, after he outlasted Justin Rose in a sudden-death playoff to complete the career Grand Slam, McIlroy concluded his remarks to the patrons by saying that he intended to come back here and put the jacket on himself. The implication being that he wanted to join select company – Jack Nicklaus in 1965-66, Nick Faldo in 1989-90, and Tiger Woods in 2001-02 – as the only players to repeat as Masters champions. “I wasn’t quite correct,” McIlroy said, noting that Ridley did the honors. “I did want to come back here and prove that last year wasn’t a fluke.”The Northern Irishman, 36, overcame a double bogey on the first nine and carded two birdies on the three-hole stretch known as Amen Corner to hold off a late charge by world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler to win by a stroke and collect his sixth career major championship.Only a few puffy white clouds managed to break up the baby-blue canvas at Augusta National as McIlroy shot 1-under 71 and signed for a 72-hole total of 12-under 276 at the famed course where Bobby Jones is the co-founder and creator of the first major of the season. It was Jones who coined one of the great lines to describe what makes golf endlessly complicated yet irresistible to golfers chasing those moments when it all comes together.“Competitive golf is played mainly on a five-and-a-half-inch course – the space between your ears.” For 16 years, the Masters and McIlroy was unrequited love. But now it is the place that he can’t get enough of, spending so much time in the lead up to the Masters that he joked, “This place feels like my home course.” Indeed, on some days in the weeks before the tournament, he dropped daughter Poppy off at school in the car line, jumped on his private plane and flew to Augusta for a practice round and was home to do the dishes that evening.“I just can't believe I waited 17 years to get one Green Jacket, and I get two in a row,” he said. “I think all of my perseverance at this golf tournament over the years has really started to pay off.”McIlroy, who shared the 54-hole lead with Cameron Young, fell two behind after he tugged his tee shot at the par-3 fourth hole left and lipped out a short bogey putt. Jack Nicklaus, the six-time Green Jacket winner, had given him advice on the practice range before the tournament began. “No F---ing double bogeys.” That was McIlroy’s second in as many days. He dipped into single-digits for the tournament at 9 under when he bogeyed No. 6. The patrons groaned when the score was posted up ahead at the leaderboard behind the seventh green but he never pressed. Speaking before the tournament, McIlroy shared what a difference getting the monkey off his back last year had meant to him.“I know that I can do it now, so that should make it a little easier for me to go out and play the golf I want to play,” he said.He turned things around with birdies at Nos. 7 and 8, but Rose had shot past him reaching 12 under with four birdies before the turn.Rose looked poised to finally get both arms inside a Green Jacket, grabbing a two-stroke lead as he headed to the back nine, but Amen Corner, the three-hole stretch beginning at No. 11 still awaited and, as is customary, it played a critical role in determining a champion. Rose bogeyed Nos. 11 and 12 and made a three-putt par at No. 13. At 45, he remains the nearly-man, closing in 70, and finishing T-3 with Tyrrell Hatton (66), Russell Henley (68) and Cameron Young (73). Amen Corner was kinder to McIlroy, who made an orthodox par at the difficult 11th, the hole that he is the most over par for during his career. Then came the par-3 12th and McIlroy couldn’t figure out the swirling wind.At that moment, McIlroy remembered a tip dispensed from two-time Masters champion Tom Watson. They played a practice round in 2009, McIlroy’s first of 18 appearances at the Masters, and the wily veteran told the prodigy to wait until he felt where the wind should be and then just hit it. “You know, just hit it as soon as you can,” McIlroy said. “That's what I did on 12. It was all over the place. When I stood up on the tee, it felt like it was off the right, and I looked at the 11th flag, it was blowing right to left. But I was patient, and I waited to feel where the wind should have been coming from, and I knew it was just a perfect three-quarter 9-iron.”McIlroy planted his tee shot to 7 feet, the closest of any competitor in the final round, and made birdie. Then he mashed a 350-yard tee shot at 13 to set up another birdie and reach 13-under. That opened up a three-stroke lead for McIlroy. Scheffler chased him to the finish line. After spotting the world No. 2 a dozen strokes at the midway point, Scheffler posted a bogey-free 65 on Saturday to make up eight of those strokes. He made birdie on two of the first three holes on Sunday but the comeback stalled with 12 straight pars. He broke that streak with an improbable birdie at 15, his first birdie on either of the second nine par 5s all week. He birdied 16, too, to trim the deficit to two but couldn’t squeak out another circle on the card coming in. McIlroy shared the 18-hole lead with a 5-under 67, which led 1992 Masters champion Fred Couples to claim, “Rory may never lose this thing again after last year.”Couples looked to be prescient when McIlroy caught fire on Friday with birdies on six of his last seven holes, including a remarkable chip-in at 17, to shoot 65 and build a six-stroke lead, the largest 36-hole lead in Masters history. Scott Van Pelt, calling the action on ESPN, summed it up perfectly. “It felt like Zeus on Olympus throwing thunderbolts,” he said.But the Masters was far from over. When McIlroy walked into player dining in the locker room that evening, his European Ryder Cup teammates Shane Lowry and Hatton were lamenting how when they finished their rounds, they were trailing by one or two but an hour later they were seven behind. “I said, ‘Boys, there's a long way to go,’” McIlroy recounted. “I certainly didn't think I was home and dry after Friday night, and I knew I still needed work to do.”Through 36 holes, McIlroy had ranked 90th out of 91 in the field in driving accuracy, and true to his words, it was simply halftime as McIlroy wobbled to a 1-over 73 on Saturday, fighting a miss to the left. By the time he made bogey at 12, his lead was gone. Talk of a coronation ceremony had shifted to questions of another major meltdown but McIlroy kept things from spiraling out of control on Saturday. McIlroy conceded that “it would have been a bitter pill to swallow if I wasn't able to get myself over the finish line.”He rushed to the range on Saturday night to work on his swing path and hit two bags of balls. His mental coach, Bob Rotella, sent him a note with a couple of reminders and a day later, he proved he could win a major without his best stuff. He played Amen Corner five strokes better on Sunday than he had the day before.There were several nerve-wracking moments for McIlroy down the stretch beginning when his pitch to the 15th green hopped forward rather than spinning back and he escaped with par. "Thanking my lucky stars with that one," McIlroy said.He added a tidy up-and-down at 16 and then told himself, just four more good swings. “I made one,” he cracked. Another scrambling act at 17 secured a par before flaring his tee shot way right into the pine trees at 18 but a bogey was good enough for the victory.For the 10th straight year, the winner came out of the final pairing. With a second Green Jacket, McIlroy reached six career majors, tying him with England’s Nick Faldo and Americans Lee Trevino and Phil Mickelson.“Many people would have thought that when he got the Grand Slam, that was it, that was the plateau, that was the mountain. Now for the next two or three months after he’d done that, maybe that was the mountain. But he’s certainly reset,” Golf Channel’s Paul McGinley said. “So who’s to say he can’t keep going on? It’s always difficult to reset when you’ve climbed a mountain and it looks like he’s done it.”McIlroy reiterated on Sunday that he felt like the Grand Slam was the destination. “And I realized it wasn't,” he said.The journey continues with a second Green Jacket, his 30th career PGA Tour title, and only 11 players in the history of the game have won more majors. Now, it’s hard to argue against McIlroy as the greatest European champion of the modern age, surpassing the record of Spain's Seve Ballesteros and matching England's Faldo for majors – but with the career Grand Slam as the tiebreaker.“It's a cool conversation to be a part of,” McIlroy said. “I'm not putting a number on it, but I certainly don't want to stop here.”
